subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Across the night, the amount of REM sleep in each cycle tends to do what?
options: Only occur once at the start
questions.explain: REM periods generally lengthen and increase across the later cycles of the night.

questions.q: Evidence that circadian rhythms continue even without light cues (e.g. cave studies) suggests sleep is controlled by what?
options: Internal endogenous pacemakers as well as external cues
questions.explain: People kept from light still keep a roughly 24-hour rhythm, showing internal pacemakers also drive circadian cycles.

questions.q: A roughly 24-hour internal body cycle, such as the sleep-wake cycle, is called what?
questions.explain: A circadian rhythm is a biological cycle lasting about 24 hours, such as the sleep-wake cycle.

questions.q: The 'restoration' theory of sleep proposes that sleep does what?
options: Repairs the body and restores energy
questions.explain: The restoration theory holds that sleep allows the body and brain to repair and restore themselves.

questions.q: In Freud's theory of dreams, the hidden underlying meaning of a dream is called the what?
questions.explain: For Freud, the latent content is the hidden, unconscious meaning behind the dream's surface (manifest) content.

questions.q: Light acting as an external cue to set our body clock is an example of what?
questions.explain: Light is a zeitgeber, an external time-giver that helps synchronise the body clock to the day.

questions.q: Jet lag occurs because the body clock is out of step with what?
options: The colour of the sky only
questions.explain: Jet lag results when internal circadian rhythms are no longer synchronised with the new local day-night cycle.

questions.q: What does 'REM' sleep stand for?
questions.explain: REM stands for Rapid Eye Movement, a sleep stage marked by darting eyes and dreaming.

questions.q: Freud's theory of dreaming describes dreams as a form of what?
questions.explain: Freud argued that dreams are disguised wish fulfilment, expressing unconscious desires.

questions.q: Which hormone, released by the pineal gland, helps promote sleep?
questions.explain: Melatonin, released by the pineal gland in darkness, helps regulate and promote sleep.

questions.q: The evolutionary (adaptive) theory of sleep suggests sleep evolved mainly to do what?
options: Keep animals safe and conserve energy when inactive
questions.explain: The evolutionary theory proposes sleep keeps animals safe and conserves energy during unproductive hours.

questions.q: Roughly how long does one complete sleep cycle last in adults?
questions.explain: A full sleep cycle through the stages and REM lasts approximately 90 minutes.

questions.q: Which is a recognised treatment or self-help strategy for insomnia?
options: Good sleep hygiene, such as a regular bedtime routine
Using bright screens late at night
questions.explain: Sleep hygiene, like a consistent routine and avoiding stimulants, is a key approach to managing insomnia.

questions.q: During which stage of sleep does most vivid dreaming occur?
questions.explain: Most vivid dreaming occurs during REM (rapid eye movement) sleep.

questions.q: In which order does a typical sleep cycle progress before reaching REM?
options: Stage 1, then 2, then deep sleep, then REM
questions.explain: Sleep typically moves from light Stage 1 to Stage 2, into deep slow-wave sleep, and then into REM.

questions.q: The main internal body clock (endogenous pacemaker) that controls circadian rhythms is the what?
questions.explain: The suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus acts as the master internal clock for circadian rhythms.

questions.q: Which is an EXTERNAL influence on sleep?
options: Light and noise in the environment
questions.explain: External influences are environmental, such as light, noise and screen use, which can disrupt sleep.

questions.q: A major criticism of the activation-synthesis theory of dreaming is that it struggles to explain what?
options: Why dreams can be meaningful or recurring
questions.explain: Critics note activation-synthesis underplays why many dreams are meaningful, emotional or repeated.

questions.q: The activation-synthesis theory explains dreams as what?
options: The brain making sense of random neural activity
questions.explain: Activation-synthesis says dreams result from the brain attempting to make sense of random neural activity.

questions.q: Insomnia is best described as which kind of sleep disorder?
questions.explain: Insomnia is difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep, leading to poor or insufficient sleep.

questions.q: A striking feature of the body during REM sleep is what?
options: The muscles are paralysed while the brain is highly active
questions.explain: During REM the major muscles are effectively paralysed (atonia) even though brain activity resembles being awake.

questions.q: Which is an INTERNAL influence on sleep?
questions.explain: Internal influences include biological factors such as body temperature and hormones like melatonin.
